thread.title: Roku (ROKU) 1st Quarter Earnings: What to Expect

author: Richard Saintvilus
title: Roku (ROKU) 1st Quarter Earnings: What to Expect
text:
Roku at Nasdaq's MarketSite
Can Roku’s ( ROKU ) streaming platform exist in a world where products from tech behemoths such as Apple ( AAPL ), Amazon ( AMZN ) and Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ) continue to grow in scale? And more importantly, can it make money?
These are the main questions Roku investors (and would-be investors) want answered when the company reports first quarter fiscal 2018 earnings results after the closing bell Wednesday. In the three months that ended March, the Los Gatos, Calif.-based company is expected to deliver a loss of 15 cents per share on revenue of $127.15 million. For the full year, ending in December, the loss is expected to narrow from $2.22 a year ago to 40 cents, while full-year revenue of $674.74 million would rise 31.6% year over year.
One of the hottest IPOs in 2017, with shares skyrocketing some 400% return from the IPO price of $14 to a high in December of $56, Roku has since fallen back to earth. The shares, which closed Tuesday at $33.12, are down 43% from those highs.
The company’s fourth-quarter 2017 results, reported in mid-February, which revealed weaker-than-expected guidance, not only spooked investors about Roku’s valuation, it also sparked concerns about the company’s value proposition given the competitive landscape in which it operates. Few hardware companies (not named Apple) are able to achieve profitability and maintain margins that warrant long-term investments.
Fitbit ( FIT ) and GoPro ( GPRO ), which emerged amid much fanfare and subsequently struggled with execution, are recent hardware examples. While Roku makes set-top boxes and connectivity products to stream content from the likes of Netflix ( NFLX ) and Hulu, the company would rather be grouped differently and not be associated to that of a hardware or appliance vendor.
To that end, Roku management has placed huge bets on the company’s content distribution platform, calling it the future of the business. “A lot of people think of us as a hardware company, the only reason we sell hardware is to acquire customers ... Even investors watch TV,” CEO Anthony Wood told Business Insider last year.
For Wood’s claim to become a reality, Roku’s growth metrics must show on Wednesday that the company’s hardware performance has taken a backseat to the streaming platform. Aside from Amazon’s Fire Stick, the hardware business competes with Google’s Chromecast and the Apple TV. It’s for this reason analysts want the platform side of Roku’s business to take a bigger leap. And it’s possible that the company is ready to deliver.
Platform revenue is expected to be $66.7 million for the quarter, while hardware revenue is projected at $60.3 million. Aside from outpacing hardware, $66.7 million in platform revenue would be nearly twice what the company achieved in the year-ago quarter. Assuming the company achieves these numbers and issues confident guidance, these shares could rebound to their $50+ level. But given the stock’s volatile nature, I would much rather watch from the sidelines.
